newsitem.title: USA: Floridians to get early look at welfare reform.
newsitem.headline: Floridians to get early look at welfare reform.

text.p: Millions of Americans who receive federal government assistance are on notice that welfare as they know it will not exist after July 1, 1997, but for more than half a million Floridians the clock is ticking a little faster.
The state's sweeping $1 billion version of welfare reform begins in less than three weeks.

Passed by state lawmakers in May after a three-year trial period, Florida's Work and Gain Economic Self-Sufficiency (WAGES) programme is generally stricter than the federal welfare reform package signed last month by President Clinton. The federal law limits benefits and restricts food stamps and supplemental security insurance to U.S. citizens.
The effects of WAGES on Florida residents collecting Aid to Families with Dependent Children (AFDC), observers agree, will be revolutionary.

"This is a fundamental change in how we approach the issue of helping low income families," said Don Winstead, chief of the WAGES programme. "To call this change the most significant change in public welfare policy in over 60 years is not an overstatement."
Advocates for Florida's 560,000 AFDC families and 500,000 families receiving food stamps say support services critical to WAGES' success are not in place or already overloaded.
The 160,000 jobs that will be needed for recipients pushed off welfare over the next few years do not exist either. But the state law is set to kick in Oct. 1, ready or not.

"If I could pray for one thing it would be that that optimism (about the program's successful start) would hold forth, but I have to be really sceptical about it," said Virginia Foy, a child advocate from southeastern Florida. "There are more needs than there is money. We're all nervous."

Like federal reform, Florida's WAGES programme cuts off welfare benefits after 24 months. But the state's lifetime cap on benefits is more restrictive than Washington's, at 48 months compared with 60 under the federal plan.

Florida penalises AFDC recipients for having more children by reducing benefits for a second child and ends direct payment to teenage mothers, who will be required to live at home or with a legal guardian.
The programme is designed to make it easy for recipients to find child care and job training and extends health benefits during the transition from welfare to work.

But advocates for welfare recipients say the reality is that waiting lists for child care already clog the system and jobs are an elusive commodity, especially in rural areas. Transportation also is a problem.

While WAGES does not alter the food stamp programme, cuts in the federal package will affect 550,000 Florida families who in 1995-96 received $1.3 billion in aid. The federal law restricts receipt of food stamps to three months out of a three-year period for most able-bodied adults.
Hard hit will be legal immigrants, people who live legally in the United States and pay taxes but are not citizens.

Under federal changes, 150,000 legal immigrants receiving food stamps will become ineligible. About 50,000 elderly and disabled immigrants will get hit twice as supplemental security income payments will be cut off Jan. 1, 1997.
